clue.text: Greek character soldiers held was Roman originally

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a figure who was one of the very first Romans

indicators.note: the soldiers are said to have held the letter, so it sits inside them

parts.note: REs, men of the Royal Engineers, a regiment of British Army soldiers
mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: Soldiers captured a Greek, who had originally been a Roman citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, made plural here as REs. Remus was the twin of Romulus, the legendary founders of Rome, so he was one of the original Romans.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the twins suckled by a she-wolf founded Rome, making this twin one of its first citizens.

clue.text: Eastender boy-friend can get you down

definitions.meaning: a Cockney's way of saying 'fella', a boyfriend
a woodcutter or anyone who fells, knocking a person or tree to the ground

explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney (an Eastender, from London's East End) says 'fella' for a boyfriend this way; and one who fells brings things down.

clue.text: Ale there brewed is spirit-like

indicators.note: beer that is brewed is worked up from its ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Freshly brewed beer is a heavenly, spiritual experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewed' rearranges the eight letters of ALE THERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something airy and delicate, like a ghost or a spirit, is described as unearthly in this way.

clue.text: First lookout guy?

definitions.note: an adjective cluing a noun: the question mark signals the first, earliest kind of human

parts.note: 'cave!' (Latin 'beware') was the British schoolboy's lookout warning that a teacher was coming
a guy is a man

explanation.surface: Who was the very first sentry on watch?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave' (said KAY-vee) is old British school slang, from Latin, shouted by the pupil keeping watch. 'First' stands, loosely, for a prehistoric human.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehistoric cave-dweller is pictured as one of the earliest people.

clue.text: Overbearing in a Southern waterway

parts.note: the Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and the south coast of England

explanation.surface: Someone domineering is out on a boat in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: THE SOLENT is a busy sailing channel off Southampton in southern England; 'a' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Insolent, arrogant behaviour is rude and domineering, so the two adjectives are close synonyms.

clue.text: Place with two alternatives shaken bodily

indicators.note: the letters are shaken up like dice, so the combined pool is rearranged
two copies of the following word are wanted, so it is written twice

parts.note: or is the word that introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Someone shakes a location, given a choice of two options, physically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two alternatives' gives OR twice; 'shaken' rearranges PLACE plus OROR to give the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means relating to the physical body rather than the spirit, as bodily does.

clue.text: Heavenly person from the Orient

definitions.meaning: of the sky or of heaven
an old term for a Chinese person, from the '... Empire', a name for China

explanation.definitionFit: The word means of the sky or heaven, and was once used for a native of China, the so-called Celestial Empire.

clue.text: To exasperate is negative in any case

indicators.note: the negative word goes inside the next word, which acts as a case holding it

parts.note: no is a negative reply

explanation.surface: Saying no is irritating whatever the circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in any case' is read literally: NO sits in the case formed by ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: To exasperate someone is to irritate or vex them.

clue.text: Opts to change position

indicators.note: the letters of the word are changed around into another order

explanation.surface: Someone chooses to move to a different place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges OPTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot is a place or location, the same as a position.

clue.text: Sweet really, despite having a frightening look

definitions.text: Sweet really, despite having a frightening look

parts.words: Sweet really, despite having a frightening look
parts.note: a hard striped British sweet whose name sounds like the glaring eye of a fearsome farm animal

explanation.surface: Someone is kind at heart even though they look scary.
explanation.walkthrough: A bull's-eye is a round, striped British boiled sweet; a bull's eye is a menacing thing to meet, hence the 'frightening look'.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a traditional peppermint boiled sweet is also the eye of an angry farm beast.

clue.text: Quick to disport oneself in exercising

indicators.note: the frolic sits inside the exercise abbreviation

parts.note: PT is physical training, school exercise
to romp is to play boisterously

explanation.surface: Someone is eager to show off during a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: PT (physical training) is the British school name for exercise lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Prompt means done without delay, so it is a synonym of quick.

clue.text: Fish forecast

indicators.note: a thing cast is thrown about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A prediction about fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forecast' is split into 'fore' and 'cast': cast rearranges FORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe is a freshwater carp-family species, the golden form popular in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: A conservationist group maintains they're aardvarks

parts.note: NT is the National Trust, the British body conserving historic sites and landscape
to bear something is to support or maintain it

explanation.surface: A wildlife charity is looking after some African burrowing mammals.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust (NT) looks after historic houses and countryside in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark is also called the ant bear, after its termite-and-ant diet.

clue.text: Attire with which air steward Christopher is familiar

definitions.text: Attire with which air steward Christopher is familiar

parts.words: Attire with which air steward Christopher is familiar
parts.note: clothing worn aloft by aircrew; Kit is the familiar short form of the name Christopher

explanation.surface: A flight attendant called Christopher knows his uniform well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'familiar' hints that Christopher becomes Kit, and 'air' suggests the clothing worn for aviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilots' and aircrew's outfits for going aloft form the gear described.

clue.text: Feeling of the Bard under the weather?

parts.note: feeling unwell, or ill
the Bard is William Shakespeare, whose short name is Will

explanation.surface: Was Shakespeare feeling unwell?
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Bard' is the common name for Shakespeare, first name William.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostility or malice is a feeling, the sense of this hyphenated noun.

clue.text: Looked ready to drop when heading for possible failure

annotationWithheld.clue: Looked ready to drop when heading for possible failure

clue.text: Accommodating overhead?

parts.note: an apartment providing accommodation plus a cover worn on top of the head

explanation.surface: Is the upstairs room obliging?
explanation.walkthrough: A FLAT CAP is the soft peaked woollen cap traditional in northern England; a flat is accommodation and a cap sits overhead.
explanation.definitionFit: A low soft cloth hat worn on the head is joined to a word for an apartment.

clue.text: Ropes used in abundance

definitions.meaning: cords used for tying things down

explanation.definitionFit: The word means ties made of cord, and in British use plenty, as in lots of cream.

clue.text: An abstainer suffering in diplomatic service

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a person employed in an embassy

parts.note: TT is teetotal, one who abstains from alcohol
an ache is pain or suffering

explanation.surface: A teetotaller is in pain while working in an embassy.
explanation.walkthrough: TT (teetotal) is a standard abbreviation for someone who drinks no alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: A junior embassy official holds a post within the foreign service.

clue.text: All-round winner-thus far

parts.note: someone who has won every round so far in a competition, but not yet the deciding match

explanation.surface: A versatile champion so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All-round winner' suggests a versatile champion, but it means one who has won each round up to the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor who reaches the last match has beaten everyone before it.

clue.text: Miss out on doctrines

indicators.note: the letters are put out of their order, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone skips some teachings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges MISS; 'on' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Isms are beliefs or ideologies, systems of thought.

clue.text: Drop round for food

parts.note: to sag is to droop or drop
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Pop over for something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop round' looks like a visit, but gives SAG then O.
explanation.definitionFit: Sago is a starch from palm pith used in puddings.

clue.text: Free to sit up and start chewing the rag

indicators.note: the chewed rag comes at the start of the answer
chewing works the word over, so its letters are rearranged
in a down entry, up means the word is read bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: Gossiping is something you can sit and do for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SIT into TIS; 'chewing' rearranges RAG into GRA, which 'start' puts first. 'Chewing the rag' is slang for chatting.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis means without charge, so given away for nothing.

clue.text: The girl in the Spanish garb

indicators.note: the Spanish word clothes the English word, so it goes around it

parts.note: el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A girl wearing Spanish clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garb' has EL dress THE, giving E-THE-L.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethel is a girl's name.

clue.text: For example, I'm so besotted with pride

indicators.note: besotted means muddled, as if drunk, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A conceited person declares himself infatuated with self-love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'besotted' rearranges IMSO to OISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive self-regard or conceit is a kind of vanity.

clue.text: One can't get bitter about Spanish port

indicators.note: the beer goes about, around, the other letters

parts.note: bitter is a British beer, an ale
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot get a pint of bitter in a Spanish harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British draught beer. ALE goes about I and CANT (can't without its apostrophe).
explanation.definitionFit: Alicante is a Mediterranean harbour city on Spain's Costa Blanca.

clue.text: Less than a thousand in America

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
US is the United States

explanation.surface: Under a thousand people live in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'than' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Minus means less, as in five minus two.

clue.text: Vexed but showing a sign of better feeling at heart

definitions.text: Vexed but showing a sign of better feeling at heart

parts.words: Vexed but showing a sign of better feeling at heart
parts.note: annoyed, yet with a smile, a sign of good humour, sitting at the word's centre

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed but secretly cheering up.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means vexed, and the middle of the word spells GRIN, a sign of better feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Chagrined means annoyed or mortified by failure.
